findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify which child owns the integration point that passes S3's 'all-none' result into S2's scope classifier (either S2 must accept and consume an all-none flag from _inherited_child_impact, or S3 must extend the scope classifier itself — one child must own both sides of the handshake).
evidence: S3 approach: 'container whose non-closed children ALL declare none, and whose own impact is none or empty → scope none' and 'dependency_hashes / the S2 scope classifier consume that'
S2 approach: 'empty deps + the ticket's effective file-impact scope is none → none' — reads ticket state only
S2 scope: 'Out of scope: container inheritance (S3)'
S3 AC-3: 'A container whose non-closed children ALL declare none is classified scope none and survives an unrelated commit (checked: scope-classifier + validity test)'
Parent AC-3 requires this validity survival to actually work end-to-end
findings.finding: S3's AC-3 (a container whose non-closed children all declare 'none' survives an unrelated commit) requires S2's compute_validity to receive S3's 'all-none' flag, but S2 marks container inheritance out of scope and does not describe any mechanism for receiving S3's rolled-up result. S2 reads only `the ticket's effective file-impact scope` from ticket state, which will be 'undeclared' for a container that never explicitly declared none — making S3 AC-3 structurally unreachable without code that neither child fully specifies.
scenarios: A container with two 'none' children gets its attestation signed. An unrelated commit is pushed. compute_validity sees empty deps and the container's own file_impact_scope='undeclared', falls through to stale-head, and incorrectly invalidates — exactly the bug this feature is meant to fix, now reproduced at the container level.

An implementer of S2 reads only S2's spec and writes the scope classifier to read ticket state; an implementer of S3 writes _inherited_child_impact to return the all-none flag but has no call site in compute_validity to deliver it to.
findings.suggested_fix: Extend S3's scope to also update the scope classifier in manifest.py (the same file S3 already lists) so that when _inherited_child_impact returns all-none, the classifier emits scope 'none' for the container — making S3 the sole owner of the container→none promotion logic. S2 remains responsible only for the single-ticket 'none' path.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] S2 must explicitly state that a signed manifest without a `file-scope:` line is treated as `undeclared` (not `none`, not a parse error), preserving today's whole-HEAD fallback for all pre-feature attestations, and that a rolled-back deployment leaves `file-scope: none` lines ignored as unknown additive lines.

Plan: 'The declaration is part of the material fingerprint, so flipping between the three states invalidates the attestation' — addresses forward transitions only, not backward compatibility of existing attestations.

Existing pattern in manifest.py: manifest_deps returns {} for pre-ADR-0002 attestations; manifest_regver returns None for pre-stamp; manifest_disabled_builtins returns [] for pre-08af — the plan should explicitly state that absence of `file-scope:` likewise defaults to `undeclared` (preserving today's behaviour), not a parse error.

findings.location: S2 — attestation scoping; Approach section ('The declaration is part of the material fingerprint'); manifest.py build_manifest / compute_validity
scenarios: A ticket certified before this feature ships has a valid attestation with no `file-scope:` line. After the feature ships, `rebar review-plan <id> --status` is called. If the new reader treats absent `file-scope:` as an error or as `none`, the ticket's attestation validity changes without any author action — either spurious invalidity or incorrect exemption from whole-HEAD checking.

If the feature is rolled back (S2 reverted) after some tickets have been signed with `file-scope: none`, the old reader must ignore the unknown line gracefully. This is likely true given the additive-line pattern, but is unasserted in the plan.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a backward-compatibility note to S2: 'Absence of `file-scope:` in a manifest → `undeclared` (identical to today's behavior). findings.finding: The `exec` tier (1-TURN / 2-STEP / AGENT) and routing metadata (`block_threshold`, `default_posture`) for the new `no-file-impact` criterion are never specified. These are required fields in `criteria_routing.json` — verified by `validate_packaged_routing()` in registry.py — and determine how the orchestrator schedules and thresholds the criterion. The plan is silent on all three.
scenarios: S4's executor must choose an exec tier (1-TURN is cheapest; AGENT allows tool use) without guidance — if they pick the wrong tier the criterion runs in a context where it cannot access the ticket's `no_file_impact_reason` field if it requires a tool read.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a fallback specification to S4 for the inconclusive case (`insufficient` sub-answer) and for criterion execution failure — specify whether the criterion passes, coaches without asserting, or escalates, consistent with the `necessity` pattern.
evidence: Plan text: 'rubric fixtures for a correct and an incorrect assertion' — only two fixture cases, no inconclusive/failure case
plan_review_necessity.md line 56: 'an ambiguous case is `insufficient` (coach, do not assert)' — the established fallback pattern
ABSENCE: no inconclusive-case handling specified for the new criterion
findings.finding: No fallback behavior is specified for the `no-file-impact` criterion when the LLM judgment is inconclusive (`insufficient`) or the criterion execution fails. The plan's AC states 'uses LLM judgment to decide whether the assertion is correct' and requires 'rubric fixtures for a correct and an incorrect assertion' but says nothing about the inconclusive case or execution failure. Other criteria that use LLM judgment (e.g., `necessity`) specify `insufficient` as an explicit sub-answer value with a defined behavior (coach, do not assert). The new criterion has no analogous fallback.
findings.location: S4 — review criterion / AC bullet 4 ('rubric fixtures for a correct and an incorrect assertion')
scenarios: A plan declares `no_file_impact` but the reason is vague ('operator action') — the LLM cannot confidently say yes or no. Without an `insufficient` path the rubric author must invent one, risking a false positive that blocks the ticket.
A criterion execution failure (LLM timeout, parse error) has no specified degradation mode — the orchestrator's default may treat it as a finding, incorrectly blocking a legitimate `none` ticket.
findings.suggested_fix: Following the `necessity` pattern: 'an ambiguous case is `insufficient` — coach the author to add a more specific `no_file_impact_reason` but do not assert a finding; execution failure degrades to pass-not-applicable (never block on a gate infrastructure error for a new advisory criterion).'.

findings.finding: The deterministic trigger placement for the `no-file-impact` criterion is ambiguous: the plan says it fires 'deterministically by the presence of the assertion' but does not specify whether this trigger lives in the DET floor (det_lint.py, P-series), as a new rule in `overlay_triggers()` (registry.py line 444-449), or as a standard LLM-routed criterion with an `applies_at` pre-filter on `file_impact_scope == none`. These are structurally different execution paths with different caller contracts — the DET floor is pre-LLM and always runs; an `overlay_triggers()` rule gates an LLM criterion; an `applies_at` filter suppresses the criterion for non-`none` tickets but still routes it through the LLM tier.
